Third, deeper collaboration on SDG 5 data analytics, evaluation and foresight, bringing together our complementarity and complementary capacities to strengthen data systems, produce integrated evidence and analytics, and provide governments and UN country teams with stronger decision-ready knowledge. Fourth, greater operational and services delivery interoperability. This could include targeted harmonization of processes, common premises, and shared services. Today, as well as on the 3rd of December, in the course of the most recent briefing of the Secretary-General of UNAT, we did hear the right statements made, stating that the Secretariat is not empowered to make some decisions. They are the prerogatives of Member States. And we would like to underscore once again that the key role in any issues on the potential reform of the two bodies needs to be played by the Executive Boards. and the synergy between them is something that needs to be discussed intergovernmentally. In this regard, we think that the documents submitted today need to be carefully discussed intergovernmentally. We, members of the Executive Board, together with the Executive Boards of the TRIPLE Executive Boards and other interested states, need to take this on board, conduct negotiations assess whether the proposed options will make our work better or worse. Until and unless there is such a discussion, we will not be ready to propose or go along with any of the options for the reform. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Russian Federation for her statement. And I'll give the floor to Japan.

Thank you, Mr. President. At the outset, I'd like to express my sincere appreciation to Madam Executive Director for her comprehensive remark. Regarding UN initiative, Japan continuously supports the objectives and the ongoing efforts being made. As a longstanding partner of UN Women, Japan looks forward to continuing meaningful engagement in its process. In this regard, I would like to make a few comments. First, we would like to thank the UN Women Secretariat for its continued efforts to keep the Executive Board informed through information sharing on multiple occasions, including further evidence and analysis on both the potential merger scenario and on alternative options, which were recently presented to Member States. These additional analyses and information further underscore the importance of grounding the reform process in objective and careful assessment. In this regard, we wish to reiterate that achieving meaningful reform requires evidence-based analysis and careful deliberations on the benefits and costs of the reform. As discussions move forward, we will continue to remain focused on ensuring that the original mandates of both organizations are fully preserved across all options and considerations. As a final point, I would like to highlight Japan's commitment to implementing the Women, Peace and Security agenda, where UN Women plays an important role. Through its dedicated work, both at the headquarters level and frontline, UN Women has been a steadfast partner of Japan in advancing WPS agenda. Mr. President, Japan as an Executive Board member will continue to work closely with UN Women in further advancing its mandate. Before concluding, I'd also like to express my sincere appreciation to Mr. Jean-Luc Foriss for his 15 years of dedicated service to the UN Women and the Executive Board. I wish him all the very best for his new endeavor. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Japan for his remarks, and I'll give the floor to Ukraine, followed by Canada, Cuba, Spain, and Rwanda, in that order. Ukraine, you have the floor.

Mr. President, Madam Executive Director, Ukraine supports the Secretary-General's reform agenda and the objectives of the UN80 initiative. I am grateful for a very detailed briefing of the Executive Director. We agree that the UN must continue looking for ways to work better, avoid unnecessary duplication, and use its resources more effectively. At the same time, any reform should be approached carefully. Changes in structures of working methods should not affect the ability of UN entities to carry out the tasks entrusted to them by Member States. That is particularly important when we speak about UN women. Today, women and girls continue to be disproportionately affected by armed conflicts, displacement, and humanitarian crisis. At the same time, in many countries, they are also taking on a greater responsibility in their communities, economies, and public institutions. Ukraine sees it every day. Russia's continuing war of aggression has had a severe impact on Ukrainian women and girls. Millions have been displaced. Thousands of Ukrainian women and girls were killed in barbaric attacks, missiles and drone attacks against civilian population, which was verified by the UN. Many, too many women have suffered conflict-related sexual violence and other grave violations committed by Russia. What a shame, what a disgrace. At the same time, women are serving in the armed forces, they are working in public institutions, they are supporting local communities, running businesses, and taking part in Ukraine's recovery right now. This year, we adopted our third national action plan on women, peace, and security through 2030. We are also working to make sure that gender equality is taken into account in recovery and reconstruction and that survivors on conflict-related sexual violence have access to support, justice, and reparations. That is why the discussion on UN 80 matters to us. Any changes should not negatively affect the effectiveness of addressing the challenges arising from Russia's aggression against Ukraine, including the protection and empowerment of women and girls. Mr. President, Ukraine supports further discussion of practical measures that can improve the work of the UN system while preserving its ability to deliver its existing mandates. We are ready to engage constructively. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Ukraine for his remarks. I now give the floor to Canada.

Mr. President, Executive Director, Your Excellencies. Canada is very happy to participate in this session at the pivotal point for the future of the multilateral system. The United Nations is currently considering the various reform options, and while we're doing that, it is essential to safeguard the mandates and the capacities which underpin sustainable development. Canada reaffirms its support to UN Women and to its normative mandate and coordination mandate, which is a pillar of the 2030 Sustainable Development Programme. Gender equality, as well as the sexual and reproductive health and rights, remain fundamental priorities for Canada and are essential drivers for security, prosperity, and resilience. We strongly support the UN80 initiatives and the reform program by the Secretary General. We support reforms based on evidence which strengthen the effectiveness, accountability, consistency and the outcomes for the United Nations system.

President, effective reform requires careful consideration of the conditions needed for long-term success, including mandate protection, operational continuity, effectiveness and stakeholder confidence. Given that the political environment today is markedly different from the one in which UN Women was established, and that progress on gender equality remains uneven and fragile, reform should be grounded in evidence and a clear assessment of the risks and benefits. Based on the information and analysis presented to date, Canada is not able to support the proposed UNFPA/UN Women merger at this time. We therefore welcome the Secretary-General's acknowledgement that the executive boards are not currently in a position to support the proposed merger and his commitment to continue dialogue with member states, especially with regards to alternative options. Canada encourages you and women to pursue these alternatives and to keep member states informed of progress. And we remain committed to working with you and our partners to advance reforms that strengthen the UN system's effectiveness and delivery for all women and girls. Thank you. Merci.
I thank the distinguished representative of Canada for his remarks. And I'll give the floor to Chuba.

Mr. President, esteemed Director Simba Bahous, we would like to express our most sincere condolences to the people of Norway and the government of Norway, as well as the royal family, due to the death of Harald V. We would like to thank you for the joint information introduced by UN Women and the UNFPA in the framework of its executive board sessions on the initiative of UN80. We reiterate that any structural transformation should respect the principles of operational continuity, and available resources to strengthen impact on the ground, and it should also preserve the comparative advantages of each entity, as well as the multidimensional and integrated focus of development. The priorities and national needs of concerned countries should be fully respected when proposing the creation of new presences on the ground or when new functions are assigned. the possible merger of UNFPA and UN Women could carry financial benefits, but there are also risks that we must consider. This includes greater instability when it comes to financing. We believe that we are not ready to take a definitive decision with regards to a possible merger. We need more information on this. We should continue carrying out transparent and substantive consultations without imposing artificial deadlines that could compromise negotiations among Member States. Cuba will continue participating constructively in discussions on UN 80, including those that have to do with UN Women, and we will do this in line with our firm commitment to advancement of women. President, in line with this commitment, and although it would seem to stray a little bit from the goal of this meeting, we must update the Executive Board on the impacts of the blockade, and specifically the energy blockade, on Cuban women and girls. We must present this update with regards to the information provided in February. Due to the lack of electricity and goods in Cuba, the national healthcare system must delay non-urgent surgeries in order to prioritize those that are life-saving. Thousands of patients today are waiting for surgeries today. 12,000 of those are children. The life expectancy of children with cancer has dropped from 85% to 65%. The child mortality rate has risen from 4.4 for every 1,000 live births to 9.9 in 2025. These are not cold, hard facts. Behind this data, we have mothers and families that are suffering. Despite this collective punishment, we ratify our unshakable commitment to gender equality and the empowerment of women, as well as strengthening our partnership with your entity. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Cuba for her statement. And I will give the floor to Spain.

Thank you, President. Spain would like to thank UN Women for the update on its participation in UN80, and specifically the work done along with the UNFPA to identify alternatives to a possible merger. Spain firmly supports the reform process initiated by the Secretary General. We agree on the need to move towards a United Nations that is more effective, coherent, and capable of working in an integrated fashion, especially at the country level. But we consider that it is equally important that structural reforms are based on evidence, have clear added value, and above all, that they preserve and strengthen the mandates that member states have entrusted to the different entities. And from this point of view, Spain would like to be clear with respect to the possible merger between UN Women and UNFPA, we do not consider that under the current circumstances there is sufficient justification to move towards an institutional merger of these entities. analyses carried out have shown that there are important differences between their mandates, operative models and capacities, and a merger could create significant risks without having proven that this would create better results for women and girls. For Spain, the priority should be protecting and strengthening the specific mandate of UN Women in an international context where gender equality and the rights of women and girls are being subject to growing pressures. UN reform should contribute to strengthening these mandates, not to dilute them. At the same time, we believe that there is leeway to deepen the cooperation between UN Women and UNFPA without a merger. This is why we value the alternatives presented to strengthen alignment, impact and effectiveness between both entities. Spain supports moving towards a greater integration and collaboration at the country level, as well as joint programming and where there is added value to strengthen cooperation in areas such as violence against women and girls, as well as greater interoperability, shared services, and coordination between both organizations. We considered that this would respond to the goals of UN 80 in a pragmatic and results-based manner. creating greater efficiency and more integrated action, preserving specific mandates and comparative advantages. We would also like to highlight the central role of Member States and their executive boards in this process. Any future proposal should be examined by competent organs before it is elevated to the GA. This is why we are willing to continue working constructively to develop these alternatives, and we believe that the goal of this phase should be clear: deepening cooperation functional integration and efficiencies between UN Women and UNFPA, preserving their institutional autonomy and their mandates. We want an ambitious reform, but also reform that protects what's working and strengthens the capacity of the system to move forward when it comes to gender equality, rights, and empowerment for all women and girls. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished delegate of Spain for that statement. And I'll give the floor to Rwanda.

Thank you very much, Mr. President, for giving me the floor. Executive Director and your team, thank you very much for your work. We align ourself with the statement delivered on behalf of the African group. Mr. President, we thank UN Women and UNFPA for further information and analysis shared since our last session, including the options presented. This continued engagement is important as you consider carefully the implications of different approaches under the UN80 particularly the mandates of the two entities. Mr. President, Rwanda reiterates that discussions on any potential merger between UNFPA and UN Women should not be considered in isolation of the UN80 reform agenda. We further reiterate that the central role of member states in this process must be strengthened, including for ownership and.

Responsibility of this process.

For under the central consideration in these discussions is what any proposed reform will mean for delivery on the ground. Any structural reform must strengthen the ability to support program countries. We therefore encourage UN Women and UNFPA.

To further explore the alternative options presented, particularly those aimed at closer country level delivery and greater operational collaboration.

There is value in pursuing practical areas where the two entities can work more closely while gathering further evidence to inform consideration of a deeper reform. As we consider the future of these two entities, Rwanda believes that all views and perspectives should be carefully considered. In particular, the perspectives and experience of program countries must remain central to all deliberations. Ultimately, any future institutional arrangement must be guided by the capacity to strengthen delivery and impact on the ground. Finally, Mr. President, as we consider the way forward, Rwanda believes that we should take the time to listen carefully to different perspectives that have emerged through this process and to weigh them against the realities on the program on the ground. We should be mindful that the choices we make are not simply about institutional reform, but the impact it is going to have on the ground in our countries. Thank you very much.

I thank the distinguished representative of Rwanda for his comments. I now give the floor to Germany, followed by Nepal, the United Kingdom, France, and the Kingdom of the Netherlands. Germany, you have the floor.

President, Madam Executive Director, distinguished members and observers of the Executive Board, Excellencies. At the outset, I would like to express my sincere gratitude to UN Women for its important work and leadership in advancing gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls. I would like to highlight three key messages. First, it is essential that the UN can rely on a robust gender architecture. At a time when gender equality is increasingly being challenged, the UN must uphold its commitment to address structural inequality and remain steadfast in promoting gender equality. Gender equality is a human right and a prerequisite for advancing sustainable development and peace in line with the 2030 Agenda. UN Women, as the UN gender equality champion, has a vital role in driving this agenda across the United Nations. Second, we must implement reforms to make the UN system more effective. We thank UN Women and UNFPA for exploring options for enhanced alignment between the agencies. We see significant potential in strengthening integrated country-level planning. These efforts would organically combine delivery capacity and improve the impact for the people the organizations serve. Looking ahead, deeper forms of integration should remain an option, including a potential recommendation by the Executive Board at a later date regarding the proposed merger. Whatever model we pursue, we must keep our objective firmly in sight: the protection of mandates and a stronger, more coherent and more effective UN system that delivers better for women and girls on the ground. Third, Germany is committed to further advancing and to anchoring gender equality and the principle for leaving no one behind at the core of the post-2030 agenda for sustainable development. We need to ensure that progress reaches everyone, women and girls, in all their diversity. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Germany for his statement. I now give the floor to Nepal.

Thank you, Mr. President, Madam Executive Director, Excellencies. Nepal thanks the Executive Director of UN Women for her comprehensive remarks, including a focus on the dire situation in the aftermath of the recent catastrophic flash floods in my home country. We extend our sincere appreciation and gratitude to the UN Member States, UN entities, including UN Women, and the broader international community for standing in strong solidarity with Nepal at this difficult time. Nepal has consistently supported the UN80 initiative as a timely opportunity to extend and coherence, reduce fragmentation, and reimagine the United Nations that is more effective, efficient, and fit for purpose. We welcome the progress made across these three workstreams. We appreciate the substantial analytical work undertaken on both the potential merger and alternative options. Such analysis is particularly important because UNFPA and UN Women are both indispensable UN entities with distinct mandates and comparative advantages. UNFPA brings specialized leadership on sexual and reproductive health and rights, population and development, demographic analysis and gender-based violence, while UN Women advances normative support, UN system-wide coordination and operational mandates across the broader gender equality and women's rights agenda. Yet their mandates also offer important opportunities for complementarity and joint delivery, particularly in advancing gender equality and the empowerment and rights of all women and girls, ending gender-based violence and accelerating the SDGs. Mr. President, let me share the following observation. First, Nepal recognized the value of assessing complementary alternative options alongside structural measures. The alternative options demonstrate that closer alignment can be pursued within existing institutional frameworks while maintaining distinct mandates, leadership and governance arrangements. It also cautions that benefits depend on clear accountability, sustained financing, institutional commitment and careful risk management. Second, UN entity reform process must deliver impact on the ground. Any reform proposal pursued should strengthen, not weaken, the effectiveness of UNFPA and UN Women, improve country-level delivery, provide more tailored support to advance sustainable development goals, and priorities of program countries and reinforce accountability for results while preserving their distinct mandates. The alternative options assessment has identified integrated country level delivery, collaboration on ending violence against women and girls and gender-based violence, stronger SDG 5 data and analytics, and operational interoperability as strategic areas where greater complementarity could generate practical value. Third, the reform must remain member state-led, transparent, inclusive, and evidence-based. We encourage the Secretary to continue providing rigorous evidence-based assessment, including cost-benefit analysis, transition implication, and potential risk. Fourth, the ultimate measure of reform should not be institutional architects alone, but stronger country presence, better delivery on mandates, and improved lives for people we serve. Finally, reform must preserve the strengths of respective entities, strengthen national ownership and country-driven programming, protect development expertise.
I thank the distinguished delegate of Nepal for his statement. I now give the floor to the United Kingdom.

Executive Director, on behalf of the United Kingdom, I thank the Executive Director for your continued leadership of UN Women, and I pay tribute to UN Women staff working in increasingly challenging and complex environments around the world. I'd also like to express my condolences again to Nepal and all those affected by the recent flooding. At a time when conflict, humanitarian crisis and shrinking civil space continues to disproportionately affect women and girls, UN Women's mandate is more important than ever. We remain fully committed to supporting UN Women in advancing gender equality, defending hard-won gains in women's rights, and ensuring that women's voices and women's equal leadership are at the center of international responses. You have our unwavering support in this endeavour, including in tackling unacceptable violence against women and girls and sexual violence in conflict. The United Kingdom reiterates its strong commitment to the Secretary-General's UN80 reform agenda, a critical opportunity to strengthen the UN's impact and effectiveness. I make three points. First, delivery. The 2018 reform of UN development system achieved progress. However, we expect UN leadership to fully deliver this agenda. Key priorities include reconfiguring UN country teams and ensuring all UN development system work adheres to cooperation frameworks. Delivery should be improved through system-wide shared services and common enablers, notably technology and data. By consolidating and modernizing back office functions, the UN can build a leaner, more effective and resilient operational backbone. To support these efforts, it is crucial to empower resident coordinators to lead one UN teams. Second, mandates. Institutional change must not undermine mandates entrusted to UN entities by member states. We have stood in union with other member states in calling for the preservation of distinct SRHR and gender equality mandates, and we are supportive of the work packages under UN system coherence and impact. Minimising disruption to ongoing operations, mitigating risks and protecting accountability mechanisms, particularly in fragile contexts, is essential. Third, evidence. Any merger decisions should be informed by strong evidence and full transparency regarding the costs of transition, the scale of efficiencies, the implications for future funding. We expect merger proposals and alternative approaches to be rigorously explored and for Member States to have adequate time and opportunity to properly review evidence and influence proposals. In conclusion, the UK supports UNAT and encourages UN leadership to fully implement the work packages, preserve mandates and build a stronger UN. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished delegate from the United Kingdom for her statement. And I'll give the floor to France.

Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, Madam Executive Director, dear colleagues, I would like to begin my statement by welcoming the work that UN Women does every day under your leadership, Madam Executive Director, dear Sima Bahous, in order to uphold equality between the sexes and the rights of women and girls. One year after the Ministerial Conference of Feminist Diplomacy in Paris, France, we'd like to reiterate its support to the triple mandate of the agency It is normative, it coordinates, and it is operative, and it pays tribute to the unshakable commitment of its teams that are working in contexts that are often very difficult. Madam Executive Director, protecting and promoting the rights of women and girls is critical to ensure the development of societies that are fair, peaceful, prosperous, and sustainable. These rights are universal. relativism of any kind cannot limit them. This led France to adopt a feminist diplomacy and new action plan on the theme women, peace and security in France support financially UN Women's work. like in Lebanon, where we support the implementation of the WPS agenda. The current reform context of our organization calls upon our collective responsibility. The legitimacy, credibility, and sustainability of our multilateral system depends on it. France, therefore, welcomes efforts to rationalize UN Women's work. And the lodestar is a better impact on the ground. For over a year, France has supported UN80, initiated by the Secretary-General, in the principle of more effective and easy to understand work to support gender equality and the health and sexual reproductive rights of women. Therefore, we support the proposal to merge UN Women and UNFPA with their mandates unchanged. Our collective appreciation on this proposal should be supported on objective elements that have been duly explained. Our board must rigorously examine the different technical and financial aspects of these scenarios to explain this to the General Assembly. They will make a decision. In the interim, and following the orientations given by the Triple Executive Board, there are several measures that may help articulate their work better and strengthen their synergies without prejudging the final decision on the merger. Friends, encourages these entities to go forward and continue with the reform. Madam Executive Director, defending the rights of women and girls is an issue of conscience and humanity, a fight against inertia and hostile forces. UN Women is at the forefront of this fight. France will continue to support you and support the United Nations to defend the rights of women and girls as well as gender equality throughout the world. The microphone is cut off.
I thank the distinguished representative of France for his statement. I now give the floor to the representative of the Kingdom of the Netherlands.

hear me? Mr. President, Madam Executive Director, distinguished members of the Board, the Kingdom of the Netherlands greatly appreciates UN Women's leadership and staff at headquarters and in the field. Your dedication, expertise and tireless efforts to advance gender equality and the empowerment of all women and girls make a tangible difference in the lives of millions every day. UN Women's triple board, the unique triple mandate, normative, coordination and operational, is essential for achieving gender equality. You help shape global norms and standards. You coordinate across the UN system to ensure coherence and accountability. And you deliver concrete results on the ground. At a time of persistent gender inequality and increasing pushback against women's and girls' rights, UN Women's voice and presence are more important than ever. To fulfill this role, it is important that UN Women is predictable, flexible, and sustainable, and has sustainable resources. Core funding enables strategic planning, rapid response, and strong normative and coordination functions. The Kingdom of the Netherlands remains a strong supporter of quality, core and multi-year funding. We regard the UN80 initiative as a key opportunity to make the UN development system more fit for purpose. We encourage UN women to continue engaging constructively in the reforms, including UN country team reconfiguration, regional reset, expertise on demand and unified services. These efforts can significantly strengthen system-wide coherence and effectiveness at country level under the leadership of the Resident Coordinator. In this regard, can you enlighten us how is UN Women currently engaging in these different work streams? And regarding a possible UNFPA-UN Women merger, We do not have sufficient evidence that a full merger would safeguard the distinct mandates of the agencies. Therefore, we are not in a position to support the merger as presented. We very much welcome the Secretary-General's recognition that the boards are not currently in a position to support merger and his comment to continue dialogue. We see promising alternatives to strengthen collaboration and improve results for women and girls globally. And therefore, my second question to UN Women: How does UN Women envisage exploring these alternative approaches? In closing, Mr. President, we look forward to working closely with UN Women and all Board members to advance our shared agenda. I thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative from the Kingdom of the Netherlands for her statement. I now give the floor to the representative of New Zealand, followed by Australia, India and Fiji. New Zealand, you have the floor.

Thank you very much. Executive Director, New Zealand commends UN Women for its continued leadership in advancing gender equality and the empowerment of all women and girls in an increasingly complex global environment. In this context, UN Women's triple mandate remains more important than ever. New Zealand places particular importance on UN Women's engagement in the Pacific. Women and girls across our region continue to face disproportionate challenges, including climate-related risks, economic vulnerability, low levels of political representation, and high rates of gender-based violence. We welcome UN Women's continued work to support women's leadership, resilience, and economic empowerment in Pacific Island countries. Turning to the broader system context, New Zealand strongly supports the Secretary-General's UN80 initiative. We need a UN development system that is more focused, efficient, and coordinated, while ensuring that gender equality remains central to the UN's work. Reform efforts should strengthen delivery and impact at country level, while preserving the expertise and mandates that Member States have entrusted to UN entities. As we consider proposals under the UN80 process, New Zealand supports evidence-based reform and has carefully considered discussions regarding a potential merger of UN Women and UNFPA. While we remain committed to ambitious reform and welcome efforts to identify greater efficiencies and coherence across the system, we are not currently convinced that sufficient evidence has been presented to demonstrate that a merger would deliver efficiency gains of a scale that would outweigh the associated risks. We are also concerned that merger proposals have not adequately demonstrated how the distinct mandates, normative functions, and comparative advantages of both organisations would be protected. We would therefore welcome continued work on ongoing and alternative reform options that could strengthen coordination, improve efficiency, and enhance impact while safeguarding the unique strengths and mandates of both entities. We look forward to further analysis and discussion of these options as requested by the Executive Board. Finally, New Zealand remains concerned about the challenging funding environment facing UN Women. Core funding remains essential for UN Women to deliver on its mandate and maintain its normative leadership. We encourage all partners to continue supporting the organization through quality funding. In closing, New Zealand reaffirms its strong support for UN Women and its vital role in advancing gender equality and the empowerment of all women and girls globally. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished delegate of New Zealand for her statement. I now give the floor to Australia.

Thank you very much, Mr. President. Australia is committed to gender equality and the empowerment of all women and girls as foundations for a peaceful, stable, and prosperous world. Australia is a steadfast supporter of UN Women's vital role and triple mandate of normative leadership, UN system coordination and country level programming. Together, these functions are essential to advancing gender equality and delivering tangible outcomes for women and girls. UN Women's work to strengthen women's full and equal participation in decision making, advance economic empowerment and rights, end violence against women and girls, and implement the Women, Peace and Security agenda has made a meaningful difference in our region, the Indo-Pacific. Australia wants to see this work continue and grow stronger. Australia would like to make three points on UNADH reform. First, Australia supports ambitious and meaningful UN reform and recognises the need to strengthen coherence and efficiency across the UN system to better meet future challenges and deliver more effectively for those it serves. Any proposal for a structural merger of UN Women and UNFPA should be grounded in the broader UN agency reform agenda and supported by evidence that demonstrates improved efficiency and stronger delivery at the country level. Second, Australia reaffirms that the mandates of UN Women and UNFPA should not be reopened. These are mandates that we all agreed and are essential to achieving gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls, and in turn, achieving the Sustainable Development Goals. Any structural reform must fully safeguard UN Women's triple mandate. Third, Australia welcomes consideration of alternative approaches to strengthening coherence and efficiency across the UN system. We encourage continued assessment of practical options that enhance collaboration and performance while preserving the strength and comparative advantages of individual entities. As a longstanding partner of UN Women, Australia remains committed to reforms that protect its critical functions and mandates, preserve delivery and strengthen the UN system's capacity to deliver for women and girls. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Australia for his statement. And I will give the floor to India.

Thank you, Mr. President. We thank the Executive Director for a comprehensive brief this morning. Mr. President, amid tightening global fiscal resources, UN women should be guarded against dilution of resources across peripheral areas. In this regard, we underscore that flexible resources remain essential to the delivery of UN Women's mandate. India welcomes the recognition of technology as a defining frontier for gender equality. We agree that bridging the digital gender divide, ensuring women's safety online and harnessing emerging technologies for women's economic empowerment must remain central to the UN Women's normative and operational work. On the UN80 initiative, India reiterates that UN80 reform should be evidence-based, Member State-driven and transparent. Given the scale and complexity of any structural change, we would urge that decisions to scale these options be preceded by a fuller assessment with clear timelines and targets so that reforms remain grounded in demonstrated results rather than projected gains. India supports a lean, non-duplicative mechanism that explicitly preserves each entity's separate mandate, accountability, and decision-making authority, avoiding the creation of a parallel governance layer. We have taken note of the assessment of the alternative options. Consistent with India's call for a pragmatic and evidence-driven approach, we urge that these lower-risk alternatives shall be tested and operationalized, and that any leap towards a potential merger shall be reserved until all risks, benefits, transition costs, and funding implications are more fully demonstrated. Mr. President, our shared objective under UNID must be to ensure that UN Women emerges as a more impact-oriented entity, delivering tangible results and empowering the lives of women and girls, particularly in developing countries. At the country level, any reform should enable a more integrated and cohesive support mechanism for the host governments and generate greater impact through pragmatic activity. India supports the broader UN objective of strengthening the coherence and impact of the UN system and remains committed to fully cooperate with other member states. I thank you, Mr. President.

I thank the distinguished delegate of India for her statement. And I will give the floor to Fiji. Fiji has two statements, group statement followed by that in their national capacity. Fiji have the floor.

Mr. President, Executive Director, Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates, I have the honor to deliver the following remarks on behalf of the 12 Pacific Island developing states represented in New York, namely the Federated States of Micronesia, Kiribati, Nauru, Palau, Papua New Guinea, the Republic of Marshall Islands, Samoa, Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu, Vanuatu, and my own country, Fiji. The Pacific Small Island Developing States support the objectives of the UN80 initiative and we recognize the importance of ensuring the United Nations system is efficient, coherent, and fit for purpose. We also engage as a region that has invested considerably alongside UN Women in building the foundations of gender equality over many years. Our governments are increasingly integrating gender equality into national climate policies and all third and all third round nationally determined contributions submitted by Pacific countries now making explicit references to gender. The Pacific Roadmap on Gender Statistics established in 2020 with the support of UN Women and the Pacific community has helped our region report more disaggregated data to the global sustainable development goal database than the global average. This work has been steadily building and depends on the institutional continuity and dedicated capacity that UN Women provides in our region. As the Board considers the pathways presented under the UN80 initiative, PCIG wants to underline that reform must account for the particular circumstances of small island developing states. The value of UN Women in the Pacific lies not only in its own programs, but equally in its role coordinating gender equality commitments across the United Nations country team, and in providing a channel through which Pacific women's organizations can contribute to national, regional, and global policy processes. These functions require dedicated institutional attention, and they should be assessed on their own terms, with full consideration of the multi-country office context through which UN Women serves our region. We have taken careful note of the analysis presented on both the potential structural merger between the United Nations Population Fund and UN Women, and the alternative options for enhanced alignment and collaboration. PC recognizes that both pathways carry implications for how the United Nations delivers on gender equality and sexual and reproductive health and rights at the country level, and we believe that whichever pathway Member States pursue, it must be guided by the demonstrated impact for women and girls, rather than institutional coherence alone. We encourage the Board to ensure that program countries are given adequate opportunity to examine and contribute to these deliberations before structural decisions are taken. We see it further underlines that reform cannot serve as a substitute for adequate and predictable core resources. Whatever efficiencies the UN80 initiative yields should be reinvested at country level delivery, particularly in the under-resourced regions such as ours. I will now move to my national capacity, and wish to add the following. Fiji reaffirms its strong and consistent support for UN Women's mandate and its unique role as the United Nations entity dedicated to gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls. Fiji supports ambitious and credible reform of the United Nations system. The UN80 initiative is a legitimate and necessary effort to improve efficiency and reduce duplication in a constrained financing environment. For Fiji, however, the core test for any reform proposal affecting UN Women remains clear. It must strengthen the ability of the United Nations to deliver for women and girls at the country level, and it must not dilute the ability in the pursuit of administrative or structural convenience. UN Women's mandate encompassing its normative, coordination and operational functions was established following extensive intergovernmental deliberation and for good reason. Gender equality cannot be advanced through mainstreaming alone. It requires a dedicated institutional home and its own leadership voice, its own accountability and the capacity to uphold the international normative framework. Any reform must safeguard UN Women's convening role and its ability to advocate independently and authoritatively for women and girls within the United Nations system and with Member States.
